{{Short description|Political Science approach to manipulate decision making process for winning}}
{{Politics sidebar}}

'''Heresthetic''' is a theoretical approach within [[political science]] that examines how political actors strategically [[Psychological manipulation|manipulate]] the structure of political situations, decision-making processes, and [[agenda-setting]] to achieve favorable outcomes even when they lack majority support.<ref name="riker5">{{cite book |last=Riker |first=William H. |author-link=William H. Riker |title=The Art of Political Manipulation |publisher=Yale University Press |year=1986 |location=New Haven, CT}}</ref> The term was coined by political scientist [[William H. Riker]] in the 1980s, combining the Greek words "hairesis" (choosing) and "rhetoric" to describe tactics beyond mere persuasion.<ref>{{cite journal |last=McLean |first=Iain C. |year=2002 |title=William H. Riker and the Invention of Heresthetic(s) |journal=British Journal of Political Science |volume=32 |issue=2 |pages=535–558 |doi=10.1017/S0007123402000224 |jstor=4092252}}</ref>

Heresthetic belongs to the tradition of [[positive political theory]], incorporating elements from [[game theory]], [[public choice theory]], [[rational choice theory]], and [[social choice theory]] to analyze strategic political behavior.<ref>{{Cite book |author=Eamonn Butler |author-link=Eamonn Butler |url=http://www.iea.org.uk/sites/default/files/publications/files/IEA%20Public%20Choice%20web%20complete%2029.1.12.pdf |title=Public Choice—A Primer |publisher=[[Institute of Economic Affairs]] |year=2012 |location=London |page=36 |type=PDF}}</ref> While [[rhetoric]] focuses on persuading others to change their preferences, heresthetic involves restructuring the political environment to achieve victory using opponents' existing preferences. Common heresthetic strategies include dimension manipulation, [[strategic voting]], [[agenda control]], and the introduction of new alternatives to split opposing coalitions.<ref>{{cite book |last=Riker |first=William H. |title=Liberalism Against Populism |publisher=Waveland Press |year=1982 |location=Long Grove, IL}}</ref> The concept has been influential in understanding political maneuvering in [[legislative politics]], [[electoral systems]], and [[constitutional design]].

==Description==
Riker argues that herestheticians win because they compel or persuade others to join them in voting or political coalitions.<ref>{{cite book|last=Riker|first=William H.|author-link=William H. Riker|title=The Theory of Political Coalitions |year=1962|publisher=Yale University Press|location=New Haven, CT}}</ref> Heresthetic focuses both on the use of [[rhetoric]] and political strategy. Riker argues that there are three vital components to heresthetic.<ref name="riker">{{cite book |last=Riker |first=William H. |author-link=William H. Riker |title=The Art of Political Manipulation |publisher=Yale University Press |year=1986 |location=New Haven, CT}}</ref>
# '''Agenda control''': political [[Principal–agent problem|agents]] may structure debate in ways that highlight favorable or eliminate undesirable [[policy]] alternatives.<ref name="smith">{{cite journal | last1 = Smith | first1 = Alex P. | last2 = Phillips | first2 = Stephen C. | year = 2021 | title = Ways and Means: Teaching Political Strategy and Heresthetic by Simulating the Budget Process | journal = Journal of Political Science Education | volume = 17 | pages = 1–11 | doi=10.1080/15512169.2021.1897602| s2cid = 236762572 }}</ref> Depending upon the order that policy options are discussed, debate can produce different outcomes, including outcomes that are not preferred by the heresthetician.<ref name="smith"/> The order of choice matters.<ref>{{cite book|last=Stoker|first=Gerry|author-link=Gerry Stoker|title=Why Politics Matters: Making Democracy Work |year=2017|publisher=Palgrave|location=New York}}</ref> Riker's concept of agenda control differs from conventional accounts of [[Agenda-setting theory|agenda-setting]] involving policy-makers, which focus on how policy-makers’ agendas are influenced by [[Exogeny|exogenous]] factors, such as the media and public opinion.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Rogers|first=Everett|author-link=Everett Rogers|author2=Dearing, James|title=Agenda-Setting Research: Where Has It Been, Where Is It Going?|journal=[[Annals of the International Communication Association]]|year=1988|volume=11|issue=1|pages=555–594 |doi=10.1080/23808985.1988.11678708}}</ref> Riker's focus is on how policy-makers affect the ordering of items on the [[political agenda]], and how that ordering can be manipulated.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Epstein | first1 = Lee | last2 = Shvetsova | first2 = Olga | year = 2002 | title = Heresthetical Maneuvering on the US Supreme Court | journal = Journal of Theoretical Politics | volume = 14 | issue = 1 | pages = 93–122 |doi=10.1177/095169280201400106| s2cid = 154391466 }}</ref>
# '''Strategic voting''': in deliberative settings herestheticians can take advantage of voting procedures to influence outcomes.<ref>{{cite book | last1 = Enelow | first1 = James M. | last2 = Hinich | first2 = Melvin J. |author-link2 = Melvin J. Hinich | title=Advances in the Spatial Theory of Voting |year=1990 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=New York}}</ref> For example, agents may vote against their own interest in the short-term to secure a better long-term position. Another element of strategic voting is [[vote trading]].<ref>{{cite book|last=Riker|first=William H.|author-link=William H. Riker|title=Liberalism Against Populism: A Confrontation Between the Theory of Democracy and the Theory of Social Choice |year=1982|publisher=Waveland Press|location=Long Grove, IL}}</ref> Policy-makers may informally trade votes with others in exchange for future votes or benefits.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/articles/A7241-2004Oct4.html|title=Vote-Trading Ethics|newspaper=The Washington Post|date=2004-10-05|access-date=2021-02-25}}</ref> [[Tactical voting|Strategic voting]] is common in legislative settings because of open rules and sequential voting procedures.
# '''Dimension manipulation''': herestheticians can manipulate the dimensionality of political decision-making by introducing new dimensions or modifying existing framing.<ref>{{cite journal | last = Edwards | first = Damian | year = 2004 | title = Divide and Conquer: Heresthetic in the Antipodes| journal = Political Science | volume = 56 | issue = 2 | pages = 65–74 |doi=10.1177/003231870405600208| s2cid = 145158963 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last = Robertson | first = David B. | year = 2006 | title = A Pivotal Politician and Constitutional Design | journal = American Political Science Review | volume = 100 | issue = 2 | pages = 303–308 |doi=10.1017/S0003055406062186| s2cid = 145452373 }}</ref> Dimension manipulation can either expand a decision-making space by reconfiguring acceptable topics of debate and policy alternatives, or shrink dimensions by eliminating certain topics or alternatives.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Kiviniemi | first1 = Marc T. | last2 = Snyder | first2 = Mark | last3 = Johnson | first3 = Bethany C. | year = 2008 | title = Motivated Dimension Manipulation in the Processing of Social Comparison Information | journal = Self and Identity | volume = 7 | issue = 3 | pages = 225–242 |pmc=3805978 |  doi=10.1080/15298860701275873| pmid = 24163591 }}</ref> The manipulation of dimensions is important because once an agent manipulates framing, it cannot be removed from debate.<ref>{{cite journal | last = Paine | first = Scott C. | year = 1989 | title = Persuasion, Manipulation, and Dimension | journal = Journal of Politics | volume = 51 | issue = 1 | pages = 36–49 |doi=10.2307/2131608| jstor = 2131608 | s2cid = 144765660 }}</ref>

These components allow herestheticians to manipulate political outcomes by structuring debate, rhetorically or structurally, to be more advantageous to their preferred position.<ref name="riker"/>

==Example==
The [[British Parliament]] is scheduling upcoming referendum votes to determine [[Scottish independence]] from the [[United Kingdom]] and if the UK should remain a member of the [[European Union]]. A [[member of parliament]] who has influence on how the votes will be structured, has a preference that Scotland will remain in union with the UK and that the UK will leave the EU. Scottish independence and the UK remaining a member of the EU is an undesirable outcome for the MP. While polling indicates that a majority of Scottish voters do not support independence, voters are more likely to support independence if the UK leaves the EU.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://foreignpolicy.com/2020/09/21/brexit-break-britain-scotland-independence/|title=Brexit Has Reignited Scotland's Push for Independence|newspaper=Foreign Policy|date=2020-09-21|access-date=2021-02-25}}</ref> In order to receive his preferred outcome, the MP seeks for the referendum votes to be held in a sequence in which Scottish independence is determined first, and then UK withdrawal from the EU. This voting sequence demonstrates how herestheticians can manipulate the decision-making process so they can win.
